Definitions

Economics

An approach to the study of human behavior.

Thinking like an economist involves:

  • Incentives: the benefits and costs of taking an action.
  • Constraints: the limits within which we make our decisions.
  • Rationality: individuals have goals and try to achieve them the best way they know how.
ECON 104
09

Definitions

Preferences

Our “taste” for certain kinds of goods and services.

  • Economists try not to rely on changes in preferences to explain things.
  • Explanations that rely on changes in incentives or constraints are economic ones.
  • Explanations that rely on preferences… are not.
  • Economics is all about: compared to what?
ECON 104
10

Optimizing within constraints

Homeowners

  • (Negative) Incentives: Increased taxes for more windows
  • Constraints: cannot change the policy itself!

William of Orange

  • Why not tax based on revenues, like we do today?
  • Did not have a well-developed tax collection service or revenue information – people might lie!
  • Needed a low-cost way to measure the wealth or income of people.
  • Number of windows correlates with the size of a house, which correlates with income.
ECON 104
11

The economic way of thinking

  • People are doing the best they can, to achieve what they want, given their constraints and incentives.
  • If you make something more costly, people do less of it.
  • If you make something less costly, people do more of it.
Incentives matter!
ECON 104
12

Overview

  • We live in a world of scarcity.
  • Scarcity implies choices
    • At the individual level, about how to use resources.
    • At the social level, about how to decide who decides.
  • Every choice has costs and benefits.
  • Incentives affect costs and benefits.
  • Institutions affect incentives.
ECON 104
13

Purposive Action

  • Individuals act with purpose – they want to achieve goals that they want to meet.
  • To achieve these goals (ends), they need means.
  • We think of these means as resources.
ECON 104
14

Scarcity and Choice

  • But there is a scarcity of resources – the means we have are limited, relative to our ends.
  • Which means we have to make choices!
  • Consider the end of wanting to score good grades in all the courses you’re taking.
  • Your time is limited: you have to choose how to spend your time.
  • But scarcity can change over time – and economic growth is great!
  • Note: scarcity can be reduced, but never eliminated!

Six centuries of falling food prices in England

How much a dozen eggs, a pound of flour, or a pound of sugar one hour of an unskilled worker’s labor could buy – 1400s vs. 2022.

Eggs (dozen)

1400s0.58 doz/hr
20224.0 doz/hr

Flour (lb)

1400s1.33 lb/hr
202250 lb/hr

Sugar (lb)

1400s0.05 lb/hr
202233.3 lb/hr
Sugar shows the most dramatic gain: over six centuries, one hour of labor buys roughly 660× more of it. Source: Gale L. Pooley & Marian L. Tupy, HumanProgress.org.
ECON 104
16

Cost and Choice

Choosing something means we must give up something.

Opportunity cost

The next best alternative you sacrifice by making a choice.

  • What is your opportunity cost of attending class today?
  • What is the opportunity cost of watching an hour of Netflix?
  • Each of you has a different opportunity cost – and it is known only to you.
ECON 104
17

There Ain’t No Such Thing as a Free Lunch

ECON 104
18

We make decisions on the margin

  • We don’t choose between all of everything of A versus all of everything of B.
  • We choose on different margins.
  • For instance: we don’t choose between spending all our day watching Netflix or all our day studying. We choose how much time to devote to each.
  • This explains why the price of diamonds is more than the price of water!
ECON 104
19

Scarcity implies competition

Scarcity implies that there would be competition, and that goods need to be rationed – and rationing can be productive, unproductive, or destructive. Back to the Ben & Jerry’s example:

1

Destructive

If you and somebody had to fight over ice cream, and you hurt each other.

2

Unproductive

Nobody benefits from you waiting in the line.

3

Productive

When you pay Ben & Jerry’s, they can do something with the money.

ECON 104
20

Exchange makes people better off!

  • People trade with each other because they expect to be better off.
  • Even if there is no production, trade creates wealth. How?
    • You buy an ice cream for $5. Why?
    • Ben & Jerry’s sells you ice cream for $5. Why?
    • You both give up something you value less for something you value more!
ECON 104
21

Institutions matter!

ECON 104
22

Institutions matter!

  • Institutions shape people’s incentives.
  • Good institutions align the incentives of people – like market exchange.
  • Bad institutions lead to unproductive or destructive use of resources.
ECON 104
23

The Seen and the Unseen

Policies can have both intended and unintended consequences – the unseen ones.

“The entire difference between a bad and a good Economist is apparent here. A bad one relies on the visible effect while the good one takes account both of the effect one can see and of those one must foresee.”

— Frédéric Bastiat
Frédéric Bastiat
ECON 104
24

Prohibition – The Seen

  • 18th Amendment – ratified in 1919 – national ban on manufacturing, transporting, and selling alcohol, 1920–1933.
  • Driven by the temperance movement’s argument that alcohol caused poverty, domestic violence, and lost workplace productivity.
  • Legal saloons closed overnight – a visible, immediate sign the law was “working.”
ECON 104
25

Prohibition – The Unseen

  • Organized crime filled the vacuum – think Al Capone in Chicago.
  • The “Iron Law of Prohibition”: banning a substance pushes producers toward more potent, more concealable versions. Distilled alcohol and fortified wines became almost ninety percent of alcohol consumption after Prohibition, compared to forty percent before – beer got squeezed out because it’s bulky to smuggle.
  • Poisoning deaths climbed as unregulated production spread – one account put the poisoned-liquor death toll at 4,154 in 1925, compared to 1,064 in 1920.

To sum up!

  • Humans act purposively – they do their best to achieve the ends they want, given their constraints and incentives.
  • We live in a world of scarcity.
  • Scarcity implies choices
    • At the individual level, about how to use resources.
    • At the social level, about how to decide who decides.
  • Every choice has costs and benefits.
  • Incentives shape costs and benefits.
  • Institutions shape incentives.
